obs: "But if, in this latter case, general words are used, which import more than seems to have been within the purview of the law... and those expressions can be restrained by others used in the same law, or in any other upon the same subject, they ought, in my opinion, to be restrained."
"the word 'whatsoever' would certainly comprehend a mortgage of a personal chattel, as well as of lands, if not restrained by other words manifesting an intent to restrain them."

“Although the words are certainly broad enough to comprehend the whole, it is believed by a majority of the court that the construction should be such as to limit the application of them to the creditors of, and subsequent purchasers from, the grantor.”
Negress Sally Henry, by William Henry, Her Father and Next Friend v. Ball

“The expressions of that part of the first section which prohibits the importation of slaves, are restricted to cases of importation for sale or to reside in this state. … nor is the court of opinion that the short time, for which she was to continue with Mrs. Rankin can satisfy the words, to reside within this state.”
Sundry Goods, Wares & Merchandises v. United States

"The expressions 'all the goods of the said traders' ... although general enough, if they stood alone, unexplained by the context, to embrace all the goods ...; are clearly restrained by the provision which immediately precedes them"
The powers to be exercised by the commissioners under these words, ought therefore to be limited to the object and purpose of the act.

“And although the words are general, and undoubtedly include officers in every branch of the public service, yet, from the general character and objects of this law, it is manifest that the attention of Congress must have been mainly directed to officers in the military service…”
"there is an equal duty to lestriet the meaning of general words, whenever it is found necessary to do so, in order to carry out the legislative intention."
"it is equally with them covered by the general term the property of the company"

"The clause requiring such provisions to be made as are necessary and proper for the prompt payment of the appropriation has reference only to the collection and application of taxes levied to meet the appropriation."
Freedman's Saving & Trust Co. v. Shepherd

"This provision was brought forward from an act of Congress, approved July 17, 1862... In the original act it immediately followed a section providing 'that all contracts made for, or orders given for the purchase of goods or supplies ... shall be promptly reported to Congress...'"; and "Although a lease, such as Bradley made, is a 'contract,' in the broadest sense of that word, we are not prepared to hold that it is of the class of contracts, the transfer of which or of any interest therein is prohibited by 3737."

"If the matter ... were wholly of interest to the States, or designed purely for the exercise of powers within the States, then properly all general expressions in the statute might be limited to States, and the intent of Congress be supported and established by the character of the subject-matter of the legislation."
Russell v. Maxwell Land Grant Co.
"The term `third persons,' as there used, *258 does not embrace all persons other than the United States and the claimants, but only those who hold superior titles"

"to restrain its operation within narrower limits than its words import if the court are satisfied that the literal meaning of its language would extend to cases which the legislature never designed to embrace in it."
"and were made more definite by the context, and by the character of the publications which had been put in evidence."
International Navigation Co. v. Farr & Bailey Manufacturing Co.
"The word \"management\" is not used without limitation, and is not, therefore, applicable in a general sense as well before as after sailing."
"That the comprehensive text of rule 23, embracing as it does \"all cases\" where a writ of error shall appear to have been sued out for mere delay, brings this case within its purview is obvious."

"the words 'any person or persons' were 'broad enough to comprehend every human being,' but he concluded that 'general words must not only be limited to cases within the jurisdiction of the state, but also to those objects to which the legislature intended to apply them.'"

“The language used by this court should be considered with the usual reasonable implications. The phrase 'at any time, … was not intended to mean at any time in the indefinite future… On the contrary the phrase at any time was necessarily intended… to mean within a reasonable time; that is, within such time as ones persuasion or other adopted means might reasonably be expected to be directly operative in causing an insurrection.”
Romero v. International Terminal Operating Co.

“jurisdiction under 1331 may still be defeated if that power has not there been exercised; in other words, if that jurisdictional grant is to be read as containing an implied exception as to cases falling within the admiralty or maritime jurisdiction.”
“It is difficult for us to believe that the Congress had in mind this type of activity when it said the thrust of conscientious objection must go to participation in war in any form.”
Federal Maritime Commission v. Pacific Maritime Ass'n
"this merely accents the importance of construing its general language in light of the Act's purposes"
Andrus v. Charlestone Stone Products Co.

"Yet the federal mining law surely was not intended to be a general real estate law"; and "the substance discovered must not only be a 'valuable mineral' within the dictionary definition of those words, but must also be the type of valuable mineral that the 1872 Congress intended to make the basis of a valid claim."
"we do not believe every conceivable arrangement that would fit a dictionary definition of an investment contract was intended to be included within the statutory definition of a security"
“Although 371 includes the words ‘in any manner or for any purpose,’ those words only modify the underlying act ‘fraud’ …”

"It is not at all unusual for this Court to conclude that the literal text of a criminal statute is broader than the coverage intended by Congress."; "[T]hough words any person or persons, [in maritime robbery statute] are broad enough to comprehend every human being[,] . . . general words must not only be limited to cases within the jurisdiction of the state, but also to those objects to which the legislature intended to apply them)."
Department of Commerce v. United States House of Representatives
“Context normally informs the meaning of a general statutory phrase and often limits its scope.”

"But that definitional view would include within the statutory phrase matters that could not possibly belong there ... And it would come close to forbidding the use of all statistics, not simply one statistical method (sampling)."
"Nor is coverage of public entities reliably signaled by speaking of any entity; any can and does mean different things depending upon the setting."
BP America Production Co. Ex Rel. Amoco Production Co. v. Burton
“But the broad terms ‘every’ and ‘any’ do not assist petitioners, as they do not broaden the ordinary meaning of the key term ‘action.’”
"But a statement that uses the word during may or may not imply other limitations as well, depending upon the context in which the statement is made."
“What matters in this example, and the Courts, is context.”
Mayo Foundation for Medical Education & Research v. United States
“Mayo’s reading does not eliminate the statute’s ambiguity as applied to working professionals.”
Kasten v. Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics Corp.
"This possibility is significant because it means that dictionary meanings, even if considered alone, do not necessarily limit the scope of the statutory phrase to written complaints."
Kasten v. Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics Corp.

“the use of the modifier any in the phrase filed any complaint suggests that Congress meant to define the word complaint expansively. Not so. The modifier any does not cause a word that is in context narrow to become broad.”
Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA
"[G]eneral terms as used on particular occasions often carry with them implied restrictions as to scope, ibid., and so courts must interpret the word any, like all other words, in context."
